pro_tips: Because the approach is so long, most parties combine Mount Tom with a full Bailey Range Traverse or a Mount Olympus expedition rather than climbing it as a standalone objective

Early-to-mid season (late June-July) trips report firmer, more continuous snow that eases travel across talus and glacier moats, at the cost of higher avalanche and stream-crossing risk; by late August the glacier is more visibly crevassed but rock sections are drier
Check the NPS Olympic 'current road conditions' and wilderness trail-conditions pages before departure — the Hoh-side approach in particular has been subject to extended road closures in recent years

The final summit-block scramble can feel harder than its nominal grade — one variation has a short 5.7-ish move (protectable with medium nuts) where other parties found an easier ~5.3 line just to the side; be ready to hunt for the path of least resistance near the top.
watch_out: The gully/slope down onto the Hubert Glacier from the Olympus massif is steep and loose enough that multiple parties have abandoned the Tom objective there — don't commit to it in wet or actively rockfalling conditions

before.approach: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded second-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route (roughly 20% grade for the first ~3 miles) and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water). At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.3 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1.3 miles to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene - the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins.

before.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (~2,550 ft, end of FR 2870), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2, which runs a gentle, mostly level mile through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River to a well-signed junction. Bear right (east, then south) onto the Royal Basin Trail #840 and settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for about 5 miles, crossing several tributary creeks — the last reliable water before the high basin — through forest that opens into wildflower meadows around the 6-mile mark, with Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw's 7,000-ft summits visible ahead. The trail steepens for the final push through switchbacks into Royal Basin, reaching Royal Lake (5,100 ft, ~7.2 mi, ~2,500 ft gain) — the established backcountry camp area (bear canisters required, no fires, permits needed May-Sept). From the lake, a climbers' path continues roughly another 0.8-1 mile and 500 ft of gain across willow flats and boulder benches to Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft, ~8 mi from the trailhead), the day-use staging area for all Needles-area objectives (camping is not permitted in the upper basin). Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread: traverse cross-country north, contouring below Mount Clark's east flank on talus and boulder benches toward Mount Walkinshaw, the northernmost peak in the Needles chain — this stretch is rough, adds roughly 1.5 miles and several hundred feet of ascending/descending sidehill travel, and involves genuine route-finding (krummholz and short cliff bands can obscure the best line, as noted by parties working this same traverse from the Gray Wolf Ridge side). Aim for the prominent talus tongue and gully system on Walkinshaw's east/southeast side — this is the 'West Side' class-3 scramble route. Ascend the loose, blocky gully (described firsthand as 'rotten Olympic shale' — notably looser than typical Cascades granite) with care, then follow class 2-3 terrain along the upper ridge, including a few short class-3 moves past steepened pinnacles, to the small (~10-ft-diameter) rocky summit at 7,378 ft. Keep parties tight and helmets on through the entire gully/ridge section — loose rock and rockfall onto climbers below are the defining hazard of this route. Total round-trip distance from the trailhead is on the order of 19 miles (matching the route's recorded 30.58 km), reflecting the extra cross-country mileage beyond Upper Royal Basin that standard figures for the closer Royal Basin peaks (Deception/Mystery, ~14 mi RT) don't include.
before.beta: The easiest route is described as a Class 3 scramble via the 'West Side' or 'Gray Wolf Ridge.' There is no maintained trail to the summit; parties leave the trail system in the 3,500-5,500 ft band and travel cross-country over open ridge and steep, brushy forest. Parties describe the west-side forest approach as the technical crux of the day due to dense brush, with class 2-3 open ridge scrambling above treeline and a final class 3 push to the small, exposed summit block.
before.face: West Side / Gray Wolf Ridge (named alternate approaches, not distinct technical faces)
hazards: Loose, rotten Olympic sandstone/shale throughout the Needles — rockfall and holds that break underweight
Multiple parallel gullies on the west side make route-finding easy to botch in cloud or whiteout
Lingering snow/ice in the approach gullies into July in heavy-snow years
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead off FR 2870; Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk, and a wilderness permit is needed for Royal Basin camping.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,550 ft at the end of FR 2870. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk, and Royal Basin camping needs a wilderness permit (quota season runs May through September).

waypoints.name: Royal Basin Trail junction
waypoints.note: Dungeness River Trail forks here; leave the river trail and climb south on the Royal Basin Trail toward Royal Creek.
waypoints.directions: Start on Upper Dungeness Trail 833.2, a gentle and nearly level mile through old growth alongside the Dungeness River to a well-signed fork. Leave the river trail and bear right, east then south, onto Royal Basin Trail 840.

waypoints.name: Royal Creek
waypoints.note: Trail parallels Royal Creek for several miles with multiple crossings; reliable water but can run high with snowmelt in early season.
waypoints.directions: Settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for roughly five miles, crossing several tributary creeks along the way. These are the last reliable water before the high basin and can run high with early-season snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Royal Lake designated camp
waypoints.note: Established sites with a composting toilet near the lake outlet; no campfires above 3,500 ft and bear canisters are required.
waypoints.directions: The forest opens into wildflower meadows around the six-mile mark, with the 7,000 ft summits of Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw in view ahead. The trail then steepens through switchbacks into Royal Basin to reach Royal Lake at 5,100 ft, about 7.2 miles in and 2,500 ft above the car. Established sites and a composting toilet sit near the outlet; bear canisters are required and no fires are allowed above 3,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Meadow
waypoints.note: Open meadow between Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin where the trail becomes fainter; watch for the climbers' path branching toward the basin's west side.
waypoints.directions: Above the lake a climbers' path crosses willow flats and boulder benches. Tread becomes fainter through this open meadow, so watch for the path branching toward the west side of the basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Royal Basin
waypoints.note: Seasonal ranger station and the last reliable water before heading cross-country; the Needles' craggy west wall rises directly above.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the climbers' path a total of roughly 0.8 to 1 mile and 500 ft of gain above Royal Lake to Upper Royal Basin at about 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Camping is not permitted in the upper basin, but it is the staging point for every Needles objective and holds the last reliable water before the cross-country travel, with the craggy west wall of the Needles rising directly above.

waypoints.name: West-side scree/talus gully system
waypoints.note: Loose, rotten Olympic shale in several parallel gullies below the ridge; rockfall risk is high, especially with parties above — helmets recommended.
waypoints.directions: Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread. Traverse cross-country north, contouring on talus and boulder benches below Mount Clark's east flank toward Walkinshaw at the north end of the chain; this stretch adds roughly 1.5 miles of rough sidehill travel with several hundred feet of ascent and descent, and demands real route-finding since krummholz and short cliff bands hide the best line. Aim for the prominent talus tongue and gully system below the ridge, where loose, rotten Olympic shale makes rockfall the defining hazard, so keep the party tight and helmets on.

waypoints.name: Mount Walkinshaw summit
waypoints.note: Northernmost summit of the Needles, reached via class 3-4 moves up the final gully to the ridge crest; exposed, loose rock near the top.
waypoints.directions: Climb the loose, blocky gully with care, then follow Class 2-3 terrain up the ridge above, including a few short Class 3 moves past steepened pinnacles, to the small summit block roughly ten feet across at 7,378 ft. The rock is looser than typical Cascades granite, so test holds and keep the party out from under each other.

approach_variants.name: Upper Royal Basin and the north traverse under Clark
approach_variants.notes: Gentle forest mile to the signed fork, then a steady climb up the Royal Creek valley crossing tributaries — the last dependable water before the high basin. Steep switchbacks into Royal Basin, camp at the lake, then continue through the upper basin and cross-country north on talus and boulder benches beneath Clark's east flank, adding a rough mile and a half of sidehill.
hazards: Loose, rotten shale throughout the Needles, with holds that break under weight
Several parallel gullies on this flank that are easy to confuse in cloud
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully — keep the party tight, helmets on
Snow and ice in the approach gullies into July in heavy-snow years
Krummholz and short cliff bands hiding the natural line on the traverse
approach_variants.baseFinding: Walkinshaw is the northernmost peak of the Needles chain, which makes the coarse identification easy: once past Upper Royal Basin you keep contouring north below Clark's east flank until the wall on your left runs out, and the last summit before it ends is yours. The base is a prominent talus tongue running down from a gully system on the east and southeast side — it is the widest and cleanest-looking fan of loose rock on that flank and it points straight at the gully above it. Pick the tongue out from far enough back to see the whole flank at once, because several parallel gullies seam this side and choosing the wrong one in cloud is the standard error here. Climb the gully, which is blocky and rotten rather than difficult, then follow Class 2 to 3 ground along the upper ridge past a few short steepened steps to a small rocky top no more than about ten feet across. On the traverse in, krummholz patches and short cliff bands obscure the natural line and tempt you either too high or too low; hold your elevation and let the wall on your left tell you when you have arrived.

before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same loose gully and class 2-3 ridge back down to the base of the talus tongue, then retrace the cross-country traverse south below Mount Clark to Upper Royal Basin. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required on the standard West Side route, and no fixed anchors or rappel stations are known to exist on it. The loose rock that makes the gully slow on the way up makes it just as slow (if not slower) coming down; downclimb facing in on the steeper sections, test holds before weighting them, and keep helmets on for the whole party the entire way down, since Olympic 'shale' rock is rotten and prone to breaking or sliding underfoot. Once back at Upper Royal Basin, follow the climbers' path back to Royal Lake and then the maintained Royal Basin Trail #840 and Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 the full ~8 miles back to the trailhead. Given the length and elevation loss, budget real time and daylight for this descent — most parties treat the round trip as a long, full day (or a backpack with a camp at Royal Lake) rather than a quick out-and-back.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep, brushy forested slopes on Walkinshaw's west side, following intermittent deer and goat trails; described as the hardest part of the route due to dense brush.
Open ridge climbing above treeline toward a false summit around 6,537 ft, continuing along Gray Wolf Ridge toward Walkinshaw.
pitch_detail.pitch: Ridge scramble to false summit (Baldy approach)

pitch_detail.notes: A weakness through cliffs at roughly 6,200-6,300 ft allows a traverse around Walkinshaw's north side into the basin beyond, bypassing the direct summit scramble.
Final scramble to the small (~10 ft diameter) rocky summit block via the West Side or Gray Wolf Ridge line.
